e: The subject is 'One' (of the reasons), which is singular: 'One of the reasons … was the lack of clear ownership.'
A third-conditional (past unreal) requires 'would not have escalated' to match 'Had the committee acted'.
'Each' is singular and takes a singular verb: 'Each of the candidates was asked'.
Comparing a member of a group with the group requires 'any other': 'more effective than any other policy' — otherwise the policy is compared with itself.

Dangling modifier: 'Walking into the auditorium' must modify the speaker, not the stage lights. Correct: 'Walking into the auditorium, the speaker was blinded…'. The error surfaces at (B), where the wrong subject appears.
Parallelism with 'not only … but also': 'not only a gifted mathematician but also a poet of real distinction', or 'not only is a … but also writes …'. Noun phrase vs verb phrase breaks the parallel.

g: a sharp shift in consumer sentiment.
e: No error. In modern usage 'data' is widely accepted as a mass noun with a singular verb; CAT does not treat 'data suggests' as an error. Don't over-correct.
With neither…nor, the verb agrees with the nearer subject — 'advisers' (plural): 'were willing'.
'The reason … was because' is redundant; use 'The reason … was that she disagreed'.

g: By the time the rescue team arrived,
e: No error. Past perfect 'had descended' correctly marks the action completed before the team arrived.
'The committee has submitted' treats it as a singular unit; the pronoun must agree: 'its report'.
'Scarcely' pairs with 'when' (or 'before'), not 'than': 'Scarcely had the meeting begun when the fire alarm went off'.
Faulty comparison: a collection is compared with a library. Correct: 'larger than that of the British Library'.
Hypothetical (contrary-to-fact) conditions take the subjunctive 'were': 'If I were in your position'.
Prepositions take object pronouns: 'Between you and me'.
After verbs of demand/insistence, the mandative subjunctive is used: 'insisted that every student submit'.
Countable nouns take 'fewer': 'Fewer people attended'. 'Less' is for uncountable quantities.
'Along with' does not create a compound subject; the subject is 'The manager' (singular): 'is expected'.

g: He is one of those writers
e: In 'one of those writers who …', the relative pronoun 'who' refers to 'writers' (plural), so the verb is plural: 'who have never sought'.
'Affect' (verb) means to influence; 'effect' as a verb means to bring about. Correct: 'will affect every small business'.

o: Hardly anyone noticed that the clock had stopped, nor did they care.
Hardly no one noticed that the clock had stopped.
Hardly anyone noticed that the clock has stopped, and nor they cared.
Hardly anyone didn't notice that the clock had stopped.
e: A is correct: 'hardly anyone' is negative in sense, and 'nor did they care' correctly inverts. B and D are double negatives; C mixes tenses ('had noticed … has stopped') and has an ungrammatical 'and nor they cared'.

o: The proposal was accepted unanimously, which surprised everyone.
The proposal being accepted unanimously surprised everyone who were present.
The proposals acceptance unanimously surprised everyone.
Unanimously accepting the proposal, everyone was surprised by the board.
e: A is correct ('which' refers to the whole preceding clause, acceptable in standard usage). B: 'everyone … were' — 'everyone' takes singular. C: missing apostrophe and misplaced adverb. D: dangling modifier — 'everyone' didn't accept the proposal.

No error. While traditionalists prefer 'owing to' when modifying a verb, 'due to' in this position is accepted in modern standard English and is not the kind of error CAT tests. The sentence is correct.
The subject is 'quality' (singular), not 'apples': 'is excellent'.

g: was taken by the investors anyway.
e: Dangling modifier: 'Having been warned' must refer to the investors, but the subject is 'the decision'. Correct: 'Having been warned …, the investors decided to proceed anyway.'

g: Not until the final report was published
e: No error. Negative opening 'Not until …' correctly triggers inversion ('did the public learn'); past perfect 'had misled' marks the earlier action; 'them' refers to the public considered as people, acceptable here.
The subject is 'The number' (singular), separated from its verb by two modifiers: 'has prompted an inquiry'. The long gap is the trap.
No error. 'Like the economists' correctly compares people with people (policymakers); 'whose' can refer to things; past perfect 'had anticipated' is apt.

g: where the state funds most research,
e: Faulty comparison: 'Unlike in France' compares a place-context with 'American universities'. Correct: 'Unlike French universities, which depend on state funding, American universities …' or 'Unlike in France, in America universities …'.

g: not to mention the casual buyer.
e: No error. 'So convincing was the forgery that …' is a correct inversion for emphasis; 'not to mention' is idiomatic.
Parallelism: 'not only explain … but also resign'. Repeating 'that she' after 'but also' breaks the parallel structure set up after 'not only'.
Parallelism within the relative clause: 'which was conducted … and involved thousands'. 'Involving' (participle) is not parallel with 'was conducted' (finite verb).
'It is high time' is followed by the past subjunctive: 'It is high time the government addressed the shortage'.
Incomplete comparison: 'as eloquent as, if not more eloquent than, any …'. The second 'as' is missing, and the comma placement must enclose the parenthetical.
A sentence opening with 'Only after …' requires subject–auxiliary inversion in the main clause: 'did the firm admit'.
'As well as' introduces a parenthetical, not a compound subject; the subject 'The CEO' is singular: 'was present'.

g: fail to address the core issue.
e: 'Every one of them' is singular and takes a singular verb: 'fails to address'. The plural 'them' sitting next to the verb is the trap.
'People' is plural: 'the way people communicate'. The opening inversion ('Rarely has … so transformed') is correct and acts as a distraction.
No error. 'Different from' is the preferred idiom; 'so … that' correctly expresses result; 'they' clearly refers to the team members.
'It's' = 'it is'; the possessive is 'its consequences'. The split infinitive in (A) is accepted in modern English and is a decoy.
The correlative 'the more … the more …' needs parallel simple verbs: 'the more it scrutinised … the more irregularities it uncovered'. The progressive 'was uncovering' breaks the parallel.

o: Were the results to be replicated, the theory would gain wide acceptance.
Were the results replicated, the theory will gain wide acceptance.
If the results would be replicated, the theory would gain wide acceptance.
Had the results be replicated, the theory would have gained wide acceptance.
e: A correctly uses the inverted subjunctive 'Were … to be' with 'would'. B mixes subjunctive with future 'will'. C uses 'would' in the if-clause. D needs 'Had the results been replicated'.

s: Choose the sentence that is grammatically correct AND unambiguous.
o: When Priya met Anjali, she was nervous.
Priya was nervous when she met Anjali.
When she met Anjali, Priya and her sister were nervous about her.
Priya told Anjali that her proposal had been rejected.
e: B is clear: 'she' can only refer to Priya, the subject. A and D have ambiguous pronouns (who was nervous? whose proposal?). C's 'her' could refer to Priya, Anjali or the sister.

o: The reason for the delay, as well as the costs involved, were explained to the shareholders.
Neither the director nor any of the managers was able to explain the delay.
Neither of the explanations offered were convincing to the auditors.
A series of errors were responsible for the delay.
e: B: with 'neither … nor', the verb agrees with the nearer subject 'any of the managers' — 'any' here is treated as singular, so 'was' is correct. A: subject is 'the reason' → 'was explained'. C: 'neither' (singular) → 'was convincing'. D: 'A series' → 'was responsible'.

s: Choose the sentence with correct parallel structure.
o: The programme aims to reduce costs, improving quality, and the expansion of access.
The programme aims to reduce costs, improve quality, and expand access.
The programme aims at reducing costs, to improve quality, and expanding access.
The programme aims to reduce costs, quality improvement, and to expand access.
e: B keeps all three items as bare infinitives after 'to'. The other options mix infinitives, gerunds and noun phrases.

s: Choose the sentence in which the modifier is placed correctly.
o: She only ate half the cake, leaving the rest for later.
Only she ate half the cake, so the rest was for later.
She ate only half the cake, leaving the rest for later.
She ate half the cake only, the rest for later leaving.
e: 'Only' should sit immediately before what it limits — 'half the cake'. A implies she did nothing but eat; B means no one else ate; D is ungrammatical.

o: Despite of the warnings, the expedition continued.
In spite the warnings, the expedition continued.
Despite the warnings, the expedition continued.
Despite that the warnings, the expedition continued.
e: 'Despite' takes a direct object with no 'of'; 'in spite of' needs 'of'. Only C is idiomatic.
When comparing exactly two, use the comparative: 'the more qualified'.

g: whomever had rented the flat before.
e: Within its clause, the pronoun is the subject of 'had rented', so it must be 'whoever'. The preposition 'to' governs the whole clause, not the pronoun — a classic hard trap. The inversion 'Lying on the table was a letter' is correct.

g: or if they should be returned to donors.
e: Parallelism in a 'whether … or …' construction: 'whether the funds should be allocated … or returned to donors'. Switching to 'or if they should be' breaks the parallel.
